Your description did not match any emergency warning pattern in the tool I checked. That is not a clearance. The check only covers a fixed list of presentations, so if your symptoms are severe, getting worse, or new and unexplained, please contact a clinician promptly.

Reflux that lasts for years is a common reason to see a clinician. The general clinical reference (condition-gerd) explains that some reflux is normal, and that reflux becomes a disease when it causes troublesome symptoms or damage to the esophageal lining. It describes heartburn and regurgitation as the typical symptoms. I can't tell from this whether that applies to you.

The GERD guideline (guideline-gerd-initial-management-and-alarm-features) lists "alarm features" that change how the condition is assessed. The part I could read includes new symptoms starting at an older age and a family history of upper gastrointestinal cancer. It also says that when symptoms don't respond to initial treatment, a clinician will usually check adherence and timing first, then may refer for endoscopy or further testing. Please raise these points with a clinician rather than working through them alone.

The lifestyle reference (lifestyle-gerd-diet) says that cutting out all common trigger foods, such as coffee, citrus, and fried food, has weak evidence behind it. The approach it describes is working out your own triggers one at a time. It also says that weight reduction, where weight is above the healthy range, has the strongest support of any lifestyle measure.

events.question: I take omeprazole every morning.
events.answer:
Omeprazole belongs to a group of medicines called proton pump inhibitors. The GERD guideline (guideline-gerd-initial-management-and-alarm-features) describes these for reflux symptoms, but the passage I retrieved does not name omeprazole or cover your dose.

The guideline says these medicines are usually taken before a meal. It adds that timing matters as much as the medicine itself, and that a dose taken with or after food is a common reason the medicine seems not to work. It also describes an initial trial of about eight weeks, after which a clinician reviews how things are going.

Whether any of this applies to you is a question for your prescriber or a pharmacist. They can check how and when you take your medicine and whether your symptoms have responded. Please don't change your dose or timing based on this summary alone.

events.question: Lately food sometimes sticks going down.
events.answer:
**Please see a clinician soon about the food sticking.** The emergency check labelled this routine, but that label does not change what the guidance says. The GERD guideline (guideline-gerd-initial-management-and-alarm-features) lists difficulty swallowing as an alarm feature. It says these symptoms call for prompt endoscopy, a test that looks inside the gullet and stomach, rather than a further trial of reflux treatment. Your reflux history and omeprazole do not make this less important. The guideline's list also includes unintended weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools, and persistent vomiting.

**Seek emergency care now** if you cannot swallow your saliva, if food or liquid becomes completely stuck, if you are vomiting blood or passing black stools, or if you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

The retrieved passages do not say what is causing this or how it should be investigated. The condition reference (condition-gerd) notes that long-standing acid exposure can narrow the gullet and cause swallowing difficulty, but that does not tell us whether that is the cause for you. Only a clinician can assess this.

events.question: Are those two things significant?
events.answer:
Yes, the guidance treats these two symptoms as significant. Each one is on the GERD guideline's list of alarm features (guideline-gerd-initial-management-and-alarm-features). When either is present, the guideline calls for prompt endoscopy, a test that looks inside the gullet and stomach, rather than further reflux treatment on its own. Having both together makes the case for prompt assessment stronger. Please book this with a clinician soon, not at a routine visit.

The general reference (condition-gerd) says long-standing acid exposure can cause narrowing of the gullet with swallowing difficulty. It also says persistent reflux is investigated rather than assumed to be the cause. Neither passage says what is causing your symptoms in your case. Only a clinician can judge that.

**Seek emergency care now** if you cannot swallow your saliva, if food or liquid becomes completely stuck, if you are vomiting blood or passing black stools (gastrointestinal bleeding guidance), or if you have chest pain or trouble breathing. Chest pain can come from the heart even when someone has reflux, so it should always be checked urgently (red-flag-chest-pain).

events.question: What would guidance say to do about them?
events.answer:
The GERD guideline (guideline-gerd-initial-management-and-alarm-features) says that when alarm features such as difficulty swallowing or unintentional weight loss are present, the usual step is **prompt endoscopy** (a test that looks inside the gullet and stomach). It advises this instead of an empiric trial, meaning a further course of reflux treatment to see whether symptoms settle.

The same passage says weight reduction helps reflux when body weight is above the healthy range. It does not apply to weight lost without trying, which needs explaining first.

The retrieved passages do not say what the endoscopy would involve, what it might find, or what would follow. They also do not explain the cause of your symptoms. A clinician needs to assess that, so please contact your prescriber or a clinician this week and ask for prompt endoscopy. Seek emergency care right away if the symptoms in my earlier message appear.
